results.title: Estimating dynamic spatial panel data models with endogenous regressors using synthetic instruments | Journal of Geographical Systems
results.content: # Estimating dynamic spatial panel data models with endogenous regressors using synthetic instruments. Estimating dynamic spatial panel data models with endogenous regressors using synthetic instruments. The paper applies synthetic instruments, initially developed for cross-sectional regression, to estimate dynamic spatial panel data models. Reg Sci Urban Econ 42(4):727–738"); Yu and Lee 2008 Quasi-maximum likelihood estimators for spatial dynamic panel data with fixed effects when both N and T are large. Environ Plan A 45:2227–2242")), who advocated the use of synthetic instruments to eliminate endogeneity bias in cross-sectional regressions, which is here extended to GMM estimation of dynamic spatial panel models. In fact, the synthetic instruments are the fitted values resulting from regressing the endogenous regressors and their spatial lags on weighted linear combinations of subsets of orthogonal eigenvectors deriving from a symmetrical \(N\) by \(N\) contiguity matrixFootnote 6\({\mathbf{M}}\_{N}\), in which the \(m\_{ij}^{{}} ,i = 1,...,N,j = 1,...N\), take the values. Applying such a spatial filter to even a completely spatially random variable will tend to find a significant relationship and a moderately strong correlation between the random variable and the synthetic instrument because it is the outcome of a search through many candidate \({\mathbf{E}}\_{i}\) s, but with a spatially organised variable, for example, a quadratic trend surface defined by its geographic coordinates, the outcome will typically be a much more significant correlation.Footnote 8 Because spatio-temporal panel data are unlikely to be randomly distributed and almost invariably spatially organised in some way, the spatial filter can be used to obtain a synthetic instrument which is highly correlated with an endogenous variable, and thus, one has a way to generate a relevant instrumental variables that are unrelated to the error term in the data, and yet which are highly correlated with endogenous variables which are related to the error term. Consider first an estimator which applies synthetic instruments, based on \({\mathbf{M}}\_{N}\), to the endogenous variables \(\tilde{x}\_{1it} ,\tilde{x}\_{2it} ,\tilde{x}\_{3it} ,\tilde{x}\_{4it}\) their spatial lags \(W\tilde{x}\_{1it} ,W\tilde{x}\_{2it} ,W\tilde{x}\_{3it} ,W\tilde{x}\_{4it}\). One of the main problems in analysing dynamic (spatial) panel data estimated by GMM with endogenous explanatory variables is the difficulty in finding appropriate instruments. results.content: # Estimation of spatial autoregressive models with covariate measurement errors. In this paper, linear spatial autoregressive (SAR) models with covariate measurement errors are studied. Among them, Su and Jin [33] proposed the profile quasi-maximum likelihood estimation approach for partially linear SAR models, Su [32] investigated the semiparametric generalized method of moments (GMM) for semiparametric SAR models, and Ai and Zhang [1] and Sun [34]) extended the 2SLS method for partially specified spatial panel data models with fixed-effects and semiparametric varying-coefficient SAR models, respectively. For example, it can be proved that the 2SLS estimator is consistent in SAR models with measurement errors in the dependent variable but inconsistent in SAR models with covariate measurement errors. Therefore, it is of great theoretical significance and practical value to develop a robust estimation for SAR models with covariate measurement errors. With this motivation, we consider in this paper the SAR models with covariate measurement errors where is the dependent variable of unit , is a scalar autoregressive parameter, denotes the spatial weight between units and , by definition . Besides the ML-based methods, many estimation methods for regression models with covariate measurement errors can be found in the books by Fuller [15], Carroll et al. In this paper, we propose a three-stage least squares estimation method for Model (1) by introducing Berkson’s and classical types of instrumental variables, respectively. In this paper, by introducing instrumental variables, we proposed a robust estimation method for linear SAS models with covariate measurement errors. ### Higher moment estimators for linear regression models with errors in the variables. ### Robust estimation in linear regression models for longitudinal data with covariate measurement errors and outliers. ### Instrumental variable estimation in generalized linear measurement error models. * ### Bias-corrected instrumental variable estimation for spatial autoregressive models with measurement errors. In this paper, bias-corrected instrumental variable estimation methods, specifically the bias-corrected two-stage least square (2SLS) estimation and the bias-corrected asymptotically best 2SLS estimation, are proposed for spatial autoregressive (SAR) models with covariate measurement errors, utilizing available information regarding the variance of the measurement error. * ### Estimation of semiparametric varying-coefficient spatial autoregressive models with measurement errors.

results.title: Dynamic Panel Data Estimation with System-GMM
results.content: While traditional static panel data models assume that idiosyncratic errors are uncorrelated across time periods, dynamic panel models account for temporal dependencies in the data by including the lagged dependent variable as a regressor, often providing a more accurate representation of economic relationships. ## Dynamic panel data model A general form of the dynamic panel data model is expressed as follows: Yit​=β1​Yi,t−1​+β2​xit​+uit​ * Yit​: Dependent variable for individual i at time t * Yi,t−1​: Lagged dependent variable * xit​: Vector of independent variables * uit​: Error term consisting of the unobserved individual-specific effect (μi​) and the idiosyncratic error (vit​) Key characteristics of the dynamic panel model: + *Dynamic dependent variable:* A lagged dependent variable is included among the regressors + *Endogenous explanatory (right-hand) variables* that are correlated with past and possible current error terms + *Fixed individual effects:* Unobserved heterogeneity among individuals, which is another source of persistence over time + *Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation* within individual units, but not across them Including the lagged dependent variable provides a more accurate representation of the dynamic nature of the data. ## Nickell bias As discovered by Nickell (1981), including the lagged dependent variable introduces endogeneity in the model due to its correlation with the error term. This transformation introduces a negative correlation between the transformed lagged dependent variable and the error term, resulting in a downward bias. It constructs valid instruments from both lagged levels and lagged differences of the endogenous variables, estimating a system of equations, one for each time period. Specifically, the following model is estimated: Empit​=β1​Empi,t−1​+β2​Wageit​+β3​Wagei,t−1​+β4​Capit​+β5​Capi,t−1​+μi​+vit​ - Empit​: Log of employment in firm i in year t - Independent variables include both current and lag values of log wages and log capital - μi​: Fixed effects per firm * The used instruments depend on assumptions about the correlation between the independent variables and the error term. # Load the package and data # Estimate the dynamic model with Two-step System GMM dyn_model <- pgmm(log(emp) ~ lag(log(emp), 1) + lag(log(wage), 0:1) + lag(log(capital), 0:1) | lag(log(emp), 2:99) + lag(log(wage), 2:99) + lag(log(capital), 2:99), * Lags of the endogenous variables are used as instruments, specified behind the `|`.

results.title: Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†
results.content: To eliminate the first-order Nickell bias and restore valid statistical inference in panel LP regressions, we propose the split-panel jackknife (SPJ) estimator (Dhaene and Jochmans, 2015; Chudik et al., 2018) as a simple, effective, and general solution. Herbst and Johannsen (2024) focus on point estimates and investigate the finite sample bias in the time series LP model with and without (in their Appendix A.2) lagged dependent variables and then extend their discussion into panel data; they employ Bao and Ullah (2007) for analytical bias correction. These studies employ cross-country panel data and adopt the panel LP regression Eq.(15): denotes some measure of economic output, and the regressor vector includes a key variable of interest —a certain measure of financial shocks.888The first three studies adopt the panel LP method, and the fourth study Cerra and Saxena (2008) adopts the dynamic panel with distributed lag model, which also suffers the Nickell bias. Figure 4 ‣ 3 Revisiting the Aftermath of Financial Crises ‣ Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†")’s panels (A) and (B) show the IRFs of the real GDP and the unemployment rate to a typical financial shock, respectively, estimated by RR’s FE and our recommended SPJ. Quantitatively, the FE estimates show an initial GDP decline of 3% following a currency crisis, stabilizing around a 4.5% decrease after five years.121212This quantitative result closely aligns with Figure 3 in Cerra and Saxena (2008), who employ a dynamic panel with distributed lags model, which also suffers from the Nickell bias. (2021) are aware of the explicit Nickell bias and they suggested or used lagged dependent variables as IVs. We show that an asymptotic bias emerges in the FE estimator for panel LP even if no lagged dependent variables are present, which is the case in many empirical applications, for example, Chodorow-Reich et al. Among all methods for comparison, SPJ’s robustness remains under a variety of simulation settings, including the prototype model in Section C.1, panel LP with cross-sectional correlations as in Section C.2, penal LP with lagged dependent variable as in Section C.3, and some empirically oriented scenarios as in Section C.4 ‣ Appendix C Additional Simulation Results ‣ Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†").
